findings.paper_title: 26-178 Update on Accounts and External Audit 2025-26
findings.headline: Audit scale fees have increased 320% since 2021/22 and additional charges are expected
findings.detail: The PSAA scale fee for 2025/26 is £363,148, compared to £86,559 in 2021/22. Ernst & Young has advised that additional fees will be charged beyond this scale fee for work it considers additional. Additional fees for 2024/25 remain pending PSAA approval, with the council having paid only the scale fee so far, creating an uncertain future liability.
findings.matters: Rising audit costs represent a material ongoing claim on the council's finances that lenders need to understand when assessing the council's cash position.
findings.quote: The scale fee for 2025/26 is 320% more than the scale fee in 2021/22 (i.e. the last full audit pre the first disclaimed opinion). EY have indicated they expect to charge additional fees on top of this significant increase to reflect what they consider to be additional work on the audit of 2025/26.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B - Draft Annual Governance Statement 2025-26
findings.headline: Demand growth in social care, SEND and housing must be actively managed before planned MTFS savings can be realised
findings.detail: Internal analysis indicates demand growth over the Medium-Term Financial Strategy period will need active management before planned savings can be fully realised. Demand pressures particularly acute in social care, SEND and housing. Council established corporate Transformation Programme to achieve financial sustainability through service redesign and demand management.
findings.matters: Signals that MTFS savings targets may not be deliverable without proactive demand management action, raising execution risk around council's financial sustainability plans.
findings.figures: None specific in document
findings.quote: Internal analysis indicates that demand growth over the Medium-Term Financial Strategy period will need to be actively managed before planned savings can be fully realised.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B - Draft Annual Governance Statement 2025-26
findings.headline: Fair Funding Review will reduce available funding with full impact phased from 2026/27 to 2028/29
findings.detail: Government policy change will redistribute national resources and reduce Wandsworth's available funding over the medium term. Full impact will be phased in over 2026/27 to 2028/29, representing a fundamental change to national resource distribution.
findings.matters: Specific, material reduction in government funding over defined period creates structural pressure on financial sustainability and will require service efficiencies or reductions to maintain current spending.
findings.quote: The Government's Fair Funding Review will be implemented from 2026/27, with the full impact of funding redistribution phased in over the period to 2028/29. This represents a fundamental change to the distribution of national resources and is expected to reduce the level of funding available over the medium term.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B - Draft Annual Governance Statement 2025-26
findings.headline: Regulator of Social Housing issued C3 judgment finding serious failings in Safety and Quality Standard
findings.detail: Wandsworth received C3 consumer judgment on 26 February 2025 citing serious failings and significant improvement needed. Ombudsman made 49 maladministration findings in 25 determinations with 82% related to repairs, complaints, damp and mould. Council established Housing Improvement and Transformation Plan and strengthened governance through Housing Improvement Board.
findings.matters: C3 judgment indicates significant control weaknesses in major service area with revenue and capital implications. Risk of undisclosed liabilities and further regulatory intervention.
findings.figures: 25 determinations with 49 maladministration findings; 82% of cases related to complaint handling, repairs, damp and mould
findings.quote: On 26 February 2025, the Regulator of Social Housing published a C3 consumer judgement for Wandsworth, concluding that there were serious failings and that significant improvement is needed, particularly in relation to the Safety and Quality Standard.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Audit Plan Assurances
findings.headline: Building Control audit identified 2 Priority 1 findings
findings.detail: The Building Control audit resulted in 2 Priority 1 findings requiring immediate attention, alongside 6 Priority 2 and 2 Priority 3 findings. Building Control is a regulatory function, and Priority 1 findings indicate immediate compliance or safety risks.
findings.matters: Building Control deficiencies could indicate failures in regulatory oversight, safety compliance, or proper vetting of building work—all carrying legal and reputational risk.
findings.figures: 2 Priority 1 findings, 6 Priority 2, 2 Priority 3
findings.quote: Building Control Audit Final Reasonable Assurance 2 6 2

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Audit Plan Assurances
findings.headline: Internal audit function postponed or cancelled multiple planned audits due to resource constraints
findings.detail: Adult Social Care, Change and Innovation, and Resident Services each had planned audits cancelled or deferred to 2026/27 specifically because of 'limited resource availability'. Cancelled work included Homecare, Integrated Health and Social Care Services, Customer Service, and Out of Hours Emergency Services audits. The audit team prioritised higher-risk assignments instead.
findings.matters: Constrained audit capacity limits the council's ability to identify and remediate control weaknesses across operations. This weakens overall risk identification and governance. A finance director or lender depends on audit finding issues early.
findings.figures: At least 6 audits cancelled or deferred, affecting Adult Social Care, Change and Innovation, Resident Services directorates
findings.quote: limited resource availability, as noted above, with the remaining capacity prioritised to support audit assignments assessed as higher risk and more time-sensitive

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Audit Plan Assurances
findings.headline: Battersea Fields housing operation received Limited Assurance with 3 Priority 1 findings
findings.detail: The Battersea Fields RMO (Central Area), covering 512 units, received Limited Assurance from internal audit, indicating control deficiencies. It carried 3 Priority 1 findings (requiring immediate remediation), 13 Priority 2 findings, and 1 Priority 3 finding. Limited Assurance means auditors found significant control weaknesses.
findings.matters: Housing maintenance is typically a major asset and cost area for councils. Control weaknesses here could affect service quality, unit condition, tenant safety, budget execution, and asset stewardship.
findings.figures: 512 units, 3 Priority 1 findings, 13 Priority 2, 1 Priority 3
findings.quote: Battersea Fields RMO (Central Area - 512 units) Final Limited Assurance 3 13 1

findings.paper_title: Update on the Accounts and External Audit 2025-26 (Paper No. 26-178)
findings.paper_url: https://democracy.wandsworth.gov.uk/documents/s128001/26-178 Update on Accounts and External Audit 2025-26.pdf
findings.headline: Audit scale fees increased 320% from £86,559 (2021/22) to £363,148 (2025/26), with additional charges expected for 2025/26.
findings.detail: The council's audit fees have escalated significantly. On top of the scale fee of £363,148, Ernst & Young expect to charge additional fees for 2025/26 to reflect what they consider to be additional work, creating cost uncertainty. Additional fees of £118,536 have been requested for 2024/25 and are pending PSAA approval.
findings.matters: Audit fee escalation represents a material and recurring cost pressure on the council's budget; lenders need visibility on spending commitments and budget pressures.
findings.figures: Scale fee £86,559 (2021/22) to £363,148 (2025/26); additional fees £118,536 requested for 2024/25 pending PSAA approval; 2025/26 additional fees TBD
findings.quote: The scale fee for 2025/26 is 320% more than the scale fee in 2021/22 (i.e. the last full audit pre the first disclaimed opinion). EY have indicated they expect to charge additional fees on top of this significant increase to reflect what they consider to be additional work on the audit of 2025/26.

findings.paper_title: Annual Governance Report 2025/26 (Paper No. 26-179)
findings.headline: Two Priority 1 fleet management recommendations overdue; no single corporate fleet policy in place
findings.detail: Audit identified fragmented fleet policies with no single comprehensive policy covering roles, responsibilities, usage, monitoring, or compliance. No consistent approach to recording vehicle usage exists; practices vary across services with some maintaining no records. Originally due 15 September 2025, recommendations remain outstanding with revised completion date now October 2026. Draft policy is being expanded by HR but not yet implemented.
findings.matters: Absent corporate fleet governance creates tax compliance risk (P11D/HMRC issues identified), vehicle accountability gaps, and suggests lack of executive control over asset management.
findings.figures: Original due date: 15 September 2025; revised due date: October 2026; affects corporate fleet of undefined size across multiple services
findings.quote: No single, comprehensive fleet policy is in place. Existing policies are fragmented and do not provide a clear, consistent framework, leading to uncertainty among staff regarding processes and responsibilities. Recommendation (Due: 15/09/2025 | Revised: Oct 2026) Develop and implement a single corporate Fleet Management Policy.

findings.paper_title: Annual Governance Report 2025/26 (Paper No. 26-179)
findings.headline: St Joseph's Primary School: Limited assurance for procurement, asset, and income controls
findings.detail: School audit received limited assurance due to procurement governance gaps (incomplete contracts register, no competitive quotations obtained for 4 out of 5 contracts reviewed, no governing body approval), asset register not updated since 2024 with incomplete identifying information, and lettings income management with both overcharging and undercharging plus delayed invoicing (contrary to policy requiring advance billing).
findings.matters: School's governance and financial controls over spending and income are weak; indicates similar gaps may exist across other school settings managed by council.
findings.figures: Contracts register incomplete; 4 out of 5 contracts lacked competitive quotations; asset register not updated since 2024; one lettings payment outstanding at time of audit
findings.quote: The contracts register was incomplete and did not provide a comprehensive record of active contracts, and testing identified that competitive quotations were not obtained for four out of five contracts reviewed. In addition, there was no evidence that contracts had been formally reported to or approved by the Governing Body in line with financial regulations.

findings.paper_title: Annual Governance Report 2025/26 (Paper No. 26-179)
findings.headline: Building Control not charging for dangerous structures inspections; estimated £94,500 annual loss
findings.detail: Council does not charge for inspection costs incurred during standard working hours for dangerous structures inspections undertaken by inspectors outside normal hours. A fee of up to £945 should be charged per visit. With approximately 100 such requests per year, this practice (in place for approximately five years) represents unrecovered revenue. Additional issues include invoices being sent to leaseholders rather than responsible freeholders.
findings.matters: Significant unrecovered income that should be collected; indicates process failure over a five-year period with no correction.
findings.figures: Approximately 100 requests per year; £945 per visit fee; estimated annual loss ~£94,500; practice in place for approximately five years
findings.quote: Audit identified that invoices are not raised for dangerous structures inspections undertaken by inspectors (not operatives for larger work) outside normal working hours. In addition, the Councils do not charge for inspection costs incurred during standard working hours. In such cases, a fee of up to £945 should be charged per visit. It is estimated that the Councils receive approximately 100 requests for such inspections per year. This practice has been in place for approximately five years.

findings.paper_title: Annual Governance Report 2025/26 (Paper No. 26-179)
findings.headline: Building Control site inspection backlog: 1,012 instances of mandatory inspections missed
findings.detail: Audit identified a significant backlog where inspections of inactive sites had exceeded the mandatory three-month interval in 1,012 instances. These breaches were primarily driven by staffing capacity constraints and sustained workload pressures. The lack of proper inspection frequency means safety-related issues, structural defects, or changes in site conditions may not be identified.
findings.matters: Non-compliance with regulatory inspection requirements creates liability risk and potential enforcement action by Building Safety Regulator; indicates service capacity crisis in Building Control.
findings.figures: 1,012 instances where inspections exceeded three-month interval; inspections required every 28 days for active sites, at least once every three months for inactive sites
findings.quote: Analysis identified 1,012 instances in Wandsworth where inspections of inactive sites had exceeded the mandatory three‑month interval. These breaches of required inspection frequencies were primarily driven by staffing capacity constraints and sustained workload pressures.

findings.paper_title: Annual Governance Report 2025/26 (Paper No. 26-179)
findings.headline: Telecare billing breakdown: £97,000 exposure from non-invoiced services and uncollected debt
findings.detail: Audit found 34 out of 50 sampled telecare items (68%) had not been invoiced at the time of testing. Outstanding debt includes approximately £75,000 of current unpaid invoices and £25,000 recommended for write-off. Additional transactions relating to service delivery and external provider equipment had not been fully processed, meaning the full extent of financial exposure remains uncertain.
findings.matters: A large revenue stream is not being billed or collected, indicating either cash flow loss or accrual accounting issues that may not be fully captured in financial statements.
findings.figures: £75,000 outstanding unpaid invoices; £25,000 recommended for write-off; total exposure approximately £97,000; 34 out of 50 items (68%) not billed
findings.quote: A high proportion of sampled cases had not been invoiced, with 34 out of 50 items reviewed not billed at the time of audit testing. This has contributed to outstanding debt, including approximately £75,000 of current unpaid invoices and a further £25,000 recommended for write-off, bringing the total estimated exposure to around £97,000.

findings.paper_title: 26-64 WBC Proposed Additions to GF Capital Programme , item 11.
findings.paper_url: https://democracy.wandsworth.gov.uk/documents/s126017/26-64 WBC Proposed Additions to GF Capital Programme.pdf
findings.headline: Material recurring revenue cost burden from borrowing programme: £6.1m–£7.1m per annum with no identified offset
findings.detail: The paper states that for every £1m borrowed at current PWLB rates over 25 years, there is 'an ongoing revenue cost in the region of £78,000 per year'. The Committed Capital Programme borrowing (£78.6m) will cost £6.1m per year; Development Pool borrowing (£90.7m) will cost £7.1m per year if fully realised. These costs are 'deemed to be affordable' but the paper provides no detail on which revenue budgets will absorb these costs or whether offsets (savings, income growth) have been identified.
findings.matters: The Council is adding a structural revenue cost of up to £13m+ per year to its budget at a time when it states it faces 'Fair Funding' constraints and 'reduced Government funding settlements'. Unless offset by efficiencies or income, this will squeeze service budgets or require council tax rises. The paper does not address this explicitly.
findings.figures: £78,000 per £1m borrowed per year over 25 years; Committed Programme £6.1m/year; Development Pool £7.1m/year if realised
findings.quote: for every £1m of capital spend funded by external borrowing, over 25 years using the current PWLB borrowing rates, there will be an ongoing revenue cost in the region of £78,000 per year.

findings.paper_title: 26-64 WBC Proposed Additions to GF Capital Programme , item 11.
findings.paper_url: https://democracy.wandsworth.gov.uk/documents/s126017/26-64 WBC Proposed Additions to GF Capital Programme.pdf
findings.headline: Cash balances forecast to reduce materially as HRA regeneration schemes progress, limiting internal borrowing flexibility
findings.detail: The Council currently holds £508m in investments (end December 2025) but is budgeting to begin 2026/27 with 'above £430m'. The Treasury Strategy forecasts that 'investments are likely to reduce as the HRA Regeneration schemes progress and other balances fall'. The Council explicitly states that 'cash balances for internal borrowing are only available to the extent that the Council has reserves that have not yet been required for their original purpose and the availability may well reduce over the next few years'. This removes a safety valve previously available.
findings.matters: Internal borrowing has been the Council's escape hatch when external funding sources were constrained. As cash reserves diminish, that option becomes unavailable at the same time the Council is becoming structurally dependent on external borrowing. This reduces financial flexibility during any period of spending pressure or revenue shortfall.
findings.figures: £508m investments as at end December 2025; expected opening position for 2026/27 'above £430m'; decline of c.£78m in the single year
findings.quote: Cash balances for internal borrowing are only available to the extent that the Council has reserves that have not yet been required for their original purpose and the availability may well reduce over the next few years.

findings.paper_title: 26-64 WBC Proposed Additions to GF Capital Programme , item 11.
findings.paper_url: https://democracy.wandsworth.gov.uk/documents/s126017/26-64 WBC Proposed Additions to GF Capital Programme.pdf
findings.headline: Capital receipts source depleting sharply: only £13.3m forecast over five years, with Right to Buy sales dropping to minimal levels after 2027/28
findings.detail: Historically, capital receipts have been Wandsworth's principal self-funding source. The paper forecasts only £13.3m over the next five years—a significant decline from historical levels. HRA Right to Buy receipts expected in 2025/26 (£3m) relate to an accelerated application backlog; these are forecast to 'drop to minimal levels from 2027/28 onwards when the applications backlog is expected to be cleared'. This source of flexible funding is effectively exhausted.
findings.matters: Loss of capital receipts removes the Council's primary historical flexibility. Combined with CIL risks and cash pressures, the Council has fewer levers to respond to overspends or emerging capital needs without further borrowing or reserve depletion.
findings.figures: £13.3m total capital receipts forecast over five years (2025/26–2029/30); £3m HRA receipts in 2025/26; RTB sales forecast to drop to minimal levels from 2027/28
findings.quote: Limited HRA receipts are anticipated to become available for General Fund use, with £3m included in the receipt forecast for 2025/26. This increase is largely driven by the acceleration in applications from existing tenants accessing the higher discount rates that were reduced as part of the Autumn Budget statement. With the revised Right to Buy (RTB) discount levels now in play (£16,000 maximum discount in London) for all new applications post November 2024, RTB sales are expected to drop to minimal levels from 2027/28 onwards when the applications backlog is expected to be cleared.

findings.paper_title: 26-64 WBC Proposed Additions to GF Capital Programme , item 11.
findings.paper_url: https://democracy.wandsworth.gov.uk/documents/s126017/26-64 WBC Proposed Additions to GF Capital Programme.pdf
findings.headline: Government CIL relief proposals create material revenue risk to temporary accommodation and capital funding
findings.detail: The Government is consulting on temporary CIL relief for schemes delivering over 20% affordable housing (consultation closed 22 January 2026). The Council has raised 'practical concerns' about the impact, stating that 'any reduction in affordable housing delivery and CIL revenues could have significant consequences both in terms of ongoing temporary accommodation costs and financing capital investment programmes'. Since around 40% of Wandsworth's capital programme is funded by CIL, this policy creates direct risk to scheme delivery and housing cost pressures.
findings.matters: A material portion of Wandsworth's planned capital investment and its revenue budgets (temporary accommodation) depend on CIL income. Policy changes that reduce CIL collection directly threaten the council's stated plans and could force difficult decisions on housing provision.
findings.figures: Approximately 40% of capital programme funded by CIL; unclear quantum of impact if relief implemented
findings.quote: Whilst it is difficult to accurately forecast potential financial implications for the Council, it is clear that any reduction in affordable housing delivery and CIL revenues could have significant consequences both in terms of ongoing temporary accommodation costs and financing capital investment programmes, particularly in the context of reduced Government funding settlements.

findings.paper_title: 26-64 WBC Proposed Additions to GF Capital Programme , item 11.
findings.paper_url: https://democracy.wandsworth.gov.uk/documents/s126017/26-64 WBC Proposed Additions to GF Capital Programme.pdf
findings.headline: CIL funding already over-committed by £58m relative to cash received, with £11.2m projected shortfall by 2030
findings.detail: The Council has committed £154.5m of future spending to CIL-funded schemes but has received only £232.6m cumulatively as at Q3 2025/26 with expenditure of £127.1m to date. This creates a structural mismatch: over-commitment of £58m against receipts. Forecast future CIL receipts of £37.7m would still leave a shortfall of £11.2m by 31 March 2030. Critically, 50% of the five-year capital programme (£236m) depends on CIL funding.
findings.matters: Schemes have been committed to spending that exceeds cash in hand and forecast collections. Any shortfall in CIL receipts—whether from market conditions or policy changes—will force either scheme delays, further borrowing, or reserve drawdowns. Lenders assess whether planned investment can actually be delivered.
findings.figures: £232.579m gross SCIL received; £127.059m spent; £154.489m future commitments; £58.071m over-commitment; forecast £11.224m shortfall by 2030; 50% of five-year programme (£236m) CIL-funded
findings.quote: By the end of quarter three 2025/26, the gross amount of SCIL received was £232.579m. Expenditure to date funded by SCIL is £127.059m and future commitments already made to schemes approved to be funded by SCIL is a further £154.489m. To date, therefore, an over commitment of £58.071m of SCIL has been made to fund projects compared to SCIL actual receipts to date.

findings.paper_title: 26-64 WBC Proposed Additions to GF Capital Programme , item 11.
findings.paper_url: https://democracy.wandsworth.gov.uk/documents/s126017/26-64 WBC Proposed Additions to GF Capital Programme.pdf
findings.headline: Council ending decades of avoiding external borrowing and entering new £169.3m borrowing programme
findings.detail: Wandsworth has historically funded all General Fund capital from asset sales and reserves, but now proposes £127.2m external borrowing plus £42.1m invest-to-save borrowing over the five-year programme. This represents a fundamental change in financial structure. The Council explicitly states that 'unless other sources and/or external funding are identified, the Council will need to borrow to fund future General Fund capital expenditure', marking a departure from being 'currently an outlier' among authorities.
findings.matters: A shift from self-funded to borrowed capital is material to debt serviceability and revenue budget sustainability. The Council will face recurring revenue costs that were previously avoided, reducing financial flexibility.
findings.figures: £169.3m total borrowing (£127.2m external borrowing plus £42.1m invest-to-save schemes); costs estimated at £6.1m-£7.1m per annum in interest and minimum revenue provision
findings.quote: the Council is in the very unusual position of having so far avoided the need to externally borrow to fund General Fund capital investment, with internal borrowing utilised in 2024/25. It is standard practice for local authorities to borrow to fund capital investment for the benefit of the borough and Wandsworth is currently an outlier in this respect.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Policy (Paper No.26-65)
findings.headline: Investment returns declining as Bank Rate falls, narrowing income available to offset debt costs
findings.detail: Average investment return fell from 5.10% (2024/25) to 4.58% achieved (December 2025), below the 4.86% budget. Further Bank Rate cuts expected—down to 3.5% in April 2026. Lower rates reduce availability of high-yielding short-term investments and shrink the investment income that currently supports the council's net finance position.
findings.matters: Investment returns have been the council's chief financial cushion, offsetting costs. As rates fall, this income stream contracts precisely when the council will take on external debt service costs (from 2028/29). Finance directors face tightening margins; lenders should note the financial buffer from investments is eroding.
findings.figures: 2024/25 return 5.10%; 2025/26 budget 4.86%; actual/forecast 4.48%-4.58%; Bank Rate forecast 3.5% April 2026
findings.quote: The Council's overall average rate of interest on investments is 4.58% as at 31 December 2025. This is predicted to be 4.48% as at 31 March 2026. This is lower than the budgeted rate of 4.86%... The Bank Rate is forecast to fall in April 2026 to 3.5%...Therefore, it is expected that there will be fewer high yielding short term investments available.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Policy (Paper No.26-65)
findings.headline: Council shifts to external borrowing from 2028/29 onwards, requiring £165m-£263m and ending zero-debt position
findings.detail: Wandsworth currently carries zero external debt and has funded all capital projects from cash reserves. The approved capital programme will exhaust this buffer, forcing the council to borrow externally from 2028/29. The liability benchmark identifies a minimum £165m external borrowing need; the HRA capital programme alone drives £263m in borrowing requirements. This marks a fundamental shift from zero-debt to material borrower.
findings.matters: Material change to council's financial profile and creditworthiness. External borrowing introduces ongoing debt service costs that displace other spending, reduces financial flexibility, and creates rollover risk. Lenders assessing exposure note this is when Wandsworth transitions from existing investor (parking cash in their funds) to future borrowing client.
findings.figures: Current external debt £0m; projected 2028/29 borrowing need £165m-£263m
findings.quote: No new external borrowing has been undertaken in 2025/26 and the council does not expect to borrow externally until 2028/29 at the earliest. ...the Council would need to borrow £165m externally in 2028/29 to remain within the liability benchmark

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Policy (Paper No.26-65)
findings.headline: Cash reserves declining sharply while capital expenditure accelerates, forcing external borrowing earlier
findings.detail: Council cash balances falling from £567m at the start of 2025/26 to £435m expected at year-end—a £132m decline in a single year. Simultaneously, approved capital expenditure is rising from £243m (2025/26) to £486m (2028/29). This compression of cash against rising commitments will exhaust the council's financial buffer and force reliance on external borrowing.
findings.matters: Finance directors must track whether declining cash can cover commitments. Lenders assess whether liquidity contraction impairs the council's ability to absorb shocks. This trajectory indicates the council will exhaust internal funding sooner than previously forecast.
findings.figures: Cash balances £567m to £435m expected; capital expenditure £243m (2025/26) rising to £486m (2028/29)
findings.quote: The Council's cash balances at the start of the financial year were £567m. Balances were £508m at 31 December 2025 and are expected to be £435m at the end of the year. ...Actual capital expenditure is projected to rise over the next three years, in line with the current approved capital programme.

findings.paper_title: Schools Maintenance Capital Programme 2026/27 (Paper No.26-66)
findings.headline: Council committing to design and tender costs before DfE grant allocation is formally confirmed
findings.detail: The council plans to incur approximately £40,000 in design fees and procurement costs to enable delivery before the summer holidays. This work will be commissioned before formal confirmation of the DfE grant. The paper acknowledges this is "at risk" and states that if funding does not materialise as anticipated, projects will be "adjusted accordingly."
findings.matters: Pre-committing costs before funding confirmation creates financial exposure: if the DfE award is materially lower than the anticipated £2.222m, the council absorbs sunk costs or must compress the programme further.
findings.figures: £40,000 committed for design and procurement in advance of formal DfE grant confirmation; £2.401m total programme
findings.quote: This work would be commissioned and committed at risk as it is in advance of the formal approval of the DfE allocation. If the expected level of funding allocation does not materialize the number of projects being delivered will be adjusted accordingly.

findings.paper_title: Schools Maintenance Capital Programme 2026/27 (Paper No.26-66)
findings.headline: DfE school maintenance funding has not kept pace with construction inflation and remains structurally insufficient
findings.detail: The council explicitly notes that DfE grant funding has remained flat while construction costs have risen significantly. The paper states concerns that funding must be higher for several years to prevent schools being exposed to risk of closure due to maintenance issues. A substantial backlog of maintenance work exceeds available funding and is held on a reserve list.
findings.matters: Underfunded maintenance of education assets indicates a growing liability on the council's balance sheet. Persistent underfunding will force future difficult choices between service deterioration and finding alternative funding.
findings.figures: Reserve list shows projects totalling £3.7m-£3.8m that cannot be funded this year; 2025/26 DfE allocation was £2.222m
findings.quote: Grant funding from the DfE has remained consistent over the years and has not increased with consumer price index (CPI) or Retail price index (RPI) and significantly not kept pace with the high levels of construction inflation. Whilst welcomed, there still remains concerns that the funds need to be at a higher level for several years to ensure the schools and Council are not exposed to the risk of schools closing.

findings.paper_title: Revenue Budget Monitoring Q3 (Paper No.26-67)
findings.headline: The council is managing a £5.594m (2.3%) General Fund overspend by drawing on reserve balances
findings.detail: The council notes it is 'in a strong position to tackle this by deploying sensibly its healthy reserve balances.' This indicates that operating deficits are being normalized via reserve depletion rather than addressed through permanent budget corrections. Multiple service areas show structural overspends (TA, ASC, HRA) that suggest reserves may face continued drawdown if these pressures persist.
findings.matters: Reserve drawdown to cover operating deficits masks underlying structural budget issues and depletes the council's financial resilience; continued deficits would erode the 'healthy reserve balances' cited in this report
findings.figures: £5.594m overspend on £239.576m budget (2.3% variance)
findings.quote: The Council is currently projecting an overspend of £5.594m (or 2.3%) compared to the approved General Fund revenue budget of £239.576m as at Q3, a reduction of £50,000 since Q2.

findings.paper_title: Revenue Budget Monitoring Q3 (Paper No.26-67)
findings.headline: Housing repairs expenditure has overrun by £10.086m, with building safety and damp-and-mould regulation now driving additional remedial work identified through an accelerated stock survey
findings.detail: The HRA shows an £8.983m total overspend, with repairs costs (+£10.086m) as the primary driver. The council is accelerating its stock survey program targeting completion by December 2026, which is 'highlighting a number of remedial works' that further pressure repairs budgets. The report acknowledges 'more work to do' to understand whether cost increases represent base-level spend or temporary backlog.
findings.matters: Building safety and damp-and-mould remediation are regulatory-driven and will likely be sustained; housing stock repair costs represent a material long-term liability that may require continued budget increases to meet statutory obligations
findings.figures: £10.086m repairs overspend; £8.983m HRA total overspend; £9m budget increase approved; £11.4m HRA reserves forecast
findings.quote: Primarily this is linked to increased expenditure on repairs (+£10.086m) which has arisen largely as a consequence of higher cost levels and a commitment to deal with necessary repairs in a timely manner.

findings.paper_title: Revenue Budget Monitoring Q3 (Paper No.26-67)
findings.headline: Children's social care is forecasting a £3.296m overspend due to a near 10% growth in children entering care, with acknowledged risks that needs could escalate further
findings.detail: The Children's OSC is held to break-even only by management efficiencies of £2.3m that offset service overspends. Children's social care itself shows a significant £3.296m overspend. The report explicitly notes 'main risks relate to the possibility that the needs of any children increase' and that 'other children with disabilities not known to the service come into the service requiring high levels of support.'
findings.matters: Children's social care demand is volatile and can shift unpredictably; current suppression by management efficiencies masks underlying cost pressures and may not be sustainable if new high-needs children enter the system
findings.figures: £3.296m overspend; near 10% growth in children in care; £0.9m external fostering pressure; £0.9m SEN transport pressure
findings.quote: Children's social care is forecasting a £3.296m overspend position due to a near 10% growth in numbers of children coming into care in the last year.

findings.paper_title: Revenue Budget Monitoring Q3 (Paper No.26-67)
findings.headline: Care home placement costs have risen £164 per week above ending package costs, driving a £2.246m overspend in Older People and Physical Disability services
findings.detail: The council faces both higher than estimated demand for care home placements AND a significant step-up in per-unit costs. The report attributes this to market-wide social care cost inflation. This £2.246m item is the largest driver of the overall £1.968m Health overspend.
findings.matters: Structural inflation in social care unit costs suggests the council's fee rates are not keeping pace with provider costs; this is likely a persistent feature of the social care market and indicates future budget pressures
findings.figures: £164 per week cost increase on new vs ending packages; £2.246m OPDS overspend; £1.968m total Health OSC overspend
findings.quote: A £2.246m overspend is forecast in Older People and Physical Disability Services. This pressure is driven by higher than estimated demand for care home placements and the increased average cost of new packages, which are £164 per week more expensive than the packages ending.

findings.paper_title: Revenue Budget Monitoring Q3 (Paper No.26-67)
findings.headline: Temporary accommodation numbers have reached 4,764 (projected year-end) against a budget assumption of 4,018, driving an unanticipated £4.580m cost overspend
findings.detail: Current placement numbers stand at 4,711 compared to budget assumption of 4,018—a 17% overspend in units. The cost pressure was described as 'largely unanticipated, especially at the current scale' when budgets were set. While average unit costs have stabilized, the sheer volume growth is driving the overspend, which has only improved by £0.425m from Q2.
findings.matters: Temporary accommodation demand is a leading indicator of homelessness and structural housing shortage; uncontrolled growth indicates an ongoing structural cost liability that could escalate further if the Renters' Reform Act does not suppress demand as hoped
findings.figures: 4,764 projected vs 4,018 budgeted; £4.580m overspend; up from 4,147 at start of year
findings.quote: Current overall numbers accommodated in temporary accommodation are 4,711 compared to a start of year position of 4,147, compared to original budget setting assumptions of 3,996 and 3,979 respectively.

findings.paper_title: Budget and Council Tax Setting 2026/27 (Paper No.26-63)
findings.headline: Significant and rising budget gap in future years; council tax flexibility limited after 2026/27
findings.detail: Para 67 explicitly flags 'a significant and rising budget gap in future years.' The settlement removes the ability to raise council tax to close this gap: while the government has allowed unrestricted council tax increases in 2027/28 and 2028/29 (para 69), para 70 notes 'the Council will need to identify efficiencies and other sources of income to help meet the ongoing budget shortfall.'
findings.matters: The gap cannot be closed by transformation savings alone (see theme 3) or reserves (theme 2). Failure to identify new income or further efficiencies will force service cuts or significant council tax rises that may face political opposition.
findings.figures: Budget gap grows from £259.027m requirement in 2026/27 to £319.577m in 2027/28 and £322.021m in 2028/29
findings.quote: The estimated service budgets, inflation allowances, current level of assumed transformation savings and future years' grant allocations generate a significant and rising budget gap in future years

findings.paper_title: Budget and Council Tax Setting 2026/27 (Paper No.26-63)
findings.headline: Prudent borrowing required in future years to fund capital investment; impact building into budget framework
findings.detail: Para 81 states: 'The scale of investment requires prudent borrowing in future years and the impact of this is built into the budget framework and MTFS and will be kept under regular review with the aim of reducing the borrowing need where possible.'
findings.matters: New borrowing is a material liability; combined with grant losses and reserve drawdown, this signals the council is financing investment from borrowing rather than revenue surplus.
findings.figures: No figure specified; impact 'built into budget framework'
findings.quote: The scale of investment requires prudent borrowing in future years and the impact of this is built into the budget framework and MTFS and will be kept under regular review

findings.paper_title: Budget and Council Tax Setting 2026/27 (Paper No.26-63)
findings.headline: Business rates reset removes all accumulated growth since 2013/14, except ~£5m from Nine Elms
findings.detail: The fundamental reset of the business rates retention system from April 2026 removes from local retention all business rates growth accumulated since the last reset in 2013/14. Wandsworth retains only ~£5m relating to Nine Elms growth (excluding ringfenced Northern Line Extension funding).
findings.matters: Loss of accumulated growth removes a revenue source councils have historically relied on for flexibility; ties future income tightly to economic volatility.
findings.figures: ~£5m of business rates growth retained from Nine Elms; all other growth since 2013/14 removed
findings.quote: All business rates growth accumulated since the last reset in 2013/14 has been removed from local retention and absorbed into the national redistribution system. The only exception to this for Wandsworth is any growth relating to Nine Elms that isn't ringfenced to fund the Northern Line Extension. Around £5m of business rates income in 2026/27 is expected to be retained by the Council

findings.paper_title: Budget and Council Tax Setting 2026/27 (Paper No.26-63)
findings.headline: Transport for London concessionary fares levy increasing 10% to £15.0m
findings.detail: TfL levy charge expected to increase to around £15.0m in 2026/27, compared to £13.6m in 2025/26—a 10% year-on-year increase. The paper notes this reflects increased usage and inflationary increases in charges, with further volatility likely.
findings.matters: This is an externally-imposed cost over which the council has no control, eroding budget flexibility at a time of structural funding loss.
findings.quote: In 2026/27 the charge is expected to increase to around £15.0m which is a 10% increase compared to 2025/26's levy of £13.6m

findings.paper_title: Budget and Council Tax Setting 2026/27 (Paper No.26-63)
findings.headline: Adult social care and homelessness demand growth of £5.5m added in 2026/27, with further unquantified pressures expected
findings.detail: The council added £5.5m additional budget in 2026/27 to reflect latest demand estimates in social care and homelessness. Para 29 notes that 'despite this, overall demand, complexity and costs continue to rise,' with 'continuing level of uncertainty around demand pressures' requiring ongoing review.
findings.matters: These are statutory services with open-ended demand; persistent underfunding of demand growth will force either further budget growth or service rationing.
findings.figures: £5.5m demand growth in 2026/27; previous £16.1m (excluding inflation) added to 2025/26 base
findings.quote: a further £5.5m within these service areas has been added to 2026/27 reflecting latest estimates of demand... overall demand, complexity and costs continue to rise... These budgets will need to be kept under review, particularly with the continuing level of uncertainty around demand pressures

findings.paper_title: Budget and Council Tax Setting 2026/27 (Paper No.26-63)
findings.headline: Transformation Programme has identified only £14m of £45m savings target; remaining £31m still to be developed
findings.detail: The council's transformation programme aims to reduce costs by £45m per year by year three. As of this budget, only £14m of initiatives have been identified and implemented through committee budget reductions. The remaining £31m 'will be developed further as the detailed business cases are scoped out' (para 32).
findings.matters: A £31m savings gap over three years represents a significant execution risk; failure to deliver would require further reserve draws or additional council tax increases beyond the current freeze.
findings.figures: £45m annual savings target; £14m already identified; £31m remaining
findings.quote: The programme's initial ambition is to reduce the Council's costs by £45m a year ongoing in three years' time. Initiatives to deliver £14m of this have already been identified and committee budgets reduced as a result, with the remaining £31m to be developed further

findings.paper_title: Budget and Council Tax Setting 2026/27 (Paper No.26-63)
findings.headline: £38m of reserve balances required to balance 2026/27 budget, explicitly flagged as unsustainable
findings.detail: The council is using £38m of reserves to balance 2026/27 (up from £14.933m in 2025/26), with the CFO warning this 'is not a long term solution' (para 77). Para 80 states: 'unless the projected structural budget gap is addressed in other ways, the continuing use of reserve balances for this purpose will become unsustainable.'
findings.matters: Reserves are finite and at current drawdown rates will be depleted within a few years, leaving the council unable to absorb any further shocks or unfunded demand.
findings.figures: £38m reserve use in 2026/27; general reserve balance of £15.021m as of 2024/25 outturn
findings.quote: £38m of reserve balances are required to balance the budget in 2026/27... unless the projected structural budget gap is addressed in other ways, the continuing use of reserve balances for this purpose will become unsustainable

findings.paper_title: Budget and Council Tax Setting 2026/27 (Paper No.26-63)
findings.headline: Fair Funding Review removes £19m of grant in 2026/27, rising to £79m lost by end of 3-year settlement
findings.detail: Wandsworth is one of only six councils nationally (five London boroughs plus one unitary) being 'protected' at 95% funding guarantee—a 5% cash cut. The settlement redistributes resources to higher-deprivation areas, disadvantaging boroughs like Wandsworth with historically low council tax and strong tax bases. The total grant funding loss rises from £19m in 2026/27 to £79m by 2028/29.
findings.matters: This is a permanent structural loss, not temporary, directly weakening Wandsworth's revenue base and ability to service debt without raising council tax significantly.
findings.figures: £19m loss 2026/27 rising to £79m by 2028/29; protection of just £7m each year
findings.quote: Wandsworth is one of five London boroughs plus one unitary authority that have been protected with only a 95% funding guarantee i.e. a 5% cash cut... total grant funding loss of £19m in 2026/27 rising to £79m by the end of the three year settlement

findings.paper_title: Housing Revenue Account Budget (including Rents & Other Charges for Council Dwellings) (Paper No. 26-7)
findings.headline: Supervision, Management and legal costs overspend £1.7m, driven by insurance costs, disrepair case settlements, and Fox House fire costs.
findings.detail: In addition to repairs overspend, the council is running over budget on general supervision and management, with particular pressure from disrepair claims and fire-related legal/insurance costs.
findings.matters: Rising insurance and legal costs for disrepair and fire incidents signal underlying stock quality and liability exposure. This is a recurring pressure, not a one-off.
findings.figures: £1.7m overspend; insurance, disrepair cases, and Fox House fire costs are the main drivers
findings.quote: General Supervision & Management budgets are also showing an overspend of circa £1.7m with the majority of this linked to increases in insurance costs, the settlement of disrepair cases and other legal costs and the costs incurred in relation to the recent Fox House fire.

findings.paper_title: Housing Revenue Account Budget (including Rents & Other Charges for Council Dwellings) (Paper No. 26-7)
findings.headline: Cumulative impact of past government rent policy has eroded the HRA income base by £35m per annum compared to inflation-indexed baseline.
findings.detail: Between 2016–2023 the government imposed 1% rent reductions for four years and then capped the April 2023 increase at 7% instead of CPI+1% (11.1%). The paper calculates this has cost the HRA £35m per annum in lost rent roll and £200m total over the period.
findings.matters: The HRA's income trajectory was permanently damaged by policy decisions outside the council's control. This constrains borrowing capacity and reserves growth. Future rent convergence could offset this but is not guaranteed.
findings.figures: £35m per annum lost rent roll; £200m cumulative loss over the policy period; £47m estimated loss from 2023/24 7% cap over 10 years
findings.quote: The cumulative impact of this is that our rent roll, the income we generate to pay for essential services and investment, is currently £35m per annum less than it would otherwise have been.

findings.paper_title: Housing Revenue Account Budget (including Rents & Other Charges for Council Dwellings) (Paper No. 26-7)
findings.headline: Business plan contains no financial provision for fire safety measures or carbon reduction beyond existing budgets, flagging emerging unquantified pressures.
findings.detail: The council explicitly notes that future fire safety and carbon reduction commitments are not yet costed into the 30-year business plan. If building safety regulations or climate commitments increase (as expected), the HRA will face additional pressures.
findings.matters: Regulatory and policy drivers are changing faster than the council's capital programme assumes. Unfunded future obligations reduce headroom for debt service and threaten reserve adequacy.
findings.figures: Not quantified; flagged as 'significant future pressures' if current repair spend continues
findings.quote: It should however be noted that the HRA business plan has no financial provision for future fire safety measures and carbon reduction initiatives beyond those already approved within existing budgets and expected to be upgraded through cyclical stock condition works and therefore these could emerge to be significant future pressures as would any continuation of repairs spend at current levels.

findings.paper_title: Housing Revenue Account Budget (including Rents & Other Charges for Council Dwellings) (Paper No. 26-7)
findings.headline: Long-term business plan assumes £4.5m of unproven efficiency savings from 2029/30 onwards to remain viable.
findings.detail: The council states that cost pressures at current elevated levels would require 'reprioritisation of existing commitments' unless efficiency programmes deliver. A total of £4.5m in efficiencies is assumed from 2029/30 onwards from the Transformation Programme and Resident Services Directorate, but no detail is given on delivery risk or contingency if these do not land.
findings.matters: The business plan's long-term viability is dependent on achieving savings that are not yet quantified or scheduled. If the Transformation Programme under-delivers, the council will need higher borrowing or service cuts.
findings.figures: £4.5m assumed efficiencies from 2029/30 onwards
findings.quote: The Transformation Programme, the creation of the Resident Services Directorate as well as further demand management actions are expected to deliver efficiencies which have been assumed within the business plan and help to deliver an ongoing viable position. A total of £4.5m has been assumed from 2029/30 onwards.

findings.paper_title: Housing Revenue Account Budget (including Rents & Other Charges for Council Dwellings) (Paper No. 26-7)
findings.headline: Rent arrears increasing, requiring higher bad debt provisions with no clear intervention outcome stated.
findings.detail: Section 4.62 flags rising rent arrears including heating, hot water, and service charge arrears beyond normal collection rate targets. The council is increasing bad debt provisions in 2026/27 (£7.17m vs £6.27m in 2025/26) but does not specify collection rate expectations or recovery actions.
findings.matters: Rising arrears suggest tenants are struggling with affordability despite welfare support. If collection deteriorates further, rental income will fall below forecast, putting the business plan into deficit.
findings.figures: Bad debt provision rising from £6.272m (2025/26) to £7.170m (2026/27)
findings.quote: Predominantly this increase is in response to the increasing levels of rent arrears (including heating and hot water and tenants' service charge arrears) within the HRA above that normally arising as a consequence of the collection rate target for which a prudent provision for bad debts will need to be determined at year end.

findings.paper_title: Housing Revenue Account Budget (including Rents & Other Charges for Council Dwellings) (Paper No. 26-7)
findings.headline: Capital borrowing requirement jumps to £429m over four years (up from £212m estimate for repairs alone) to fund repairs, regeneration, and new housing.
findings.detail: The council forecasts borrowing of £884m over ten years split between £212m for repairs/improvements and £672m for regeneration and new housing. Over the four-year budget framework, borrowing of £429m is required. The council currently uses internal borrowing from general fund cash reserves but will need external borrowing if reserves deplete.
findings.matters: This is a material increase in debt financing. The repayment profile and interest cost assumptions are central to business plan viability. Rising borrowing for repairs (rather than development) signals structural cost escalation.
findings.quote: Borrowing of £884m is forecast in the HRA to support long-term investment over the next 10 years. This is expected to be needed in tranches matching the balance of capital spend not financed by other financing sources.

findings.paper_title: Housing Revenue Account Budget (including Rents & Other Charges for Council Dwellings) (Paper No. 26-7)
findings.headline: Regulator of Social Housing gave the council a C3 rating, triggering accelerated stock condition surveys and unbudgeted remedial spending.
findings.detail: The council has accelerated a 100% stock condition survey from five years to completion of tenanted properties by December 2026, as part of a Housing Improvement and Transformation Plan agreed with the Regulator. Surveys identify previously unreported hazards, driving reactive repairs and contributing to the revenue overspend.
findings.matters: Regulatory pressure is forcing unplanned capital and revenue expenditure ahead of schedule. The scale of remedial works remains uncertain until surveys complete, creating budget risk.
findings.figures: c.20% of stock (c.3,300 properties) surveyed to date; full survey completion deadline December 2026 for tenanted properties
findings.quote: More recently this increased investment need has been further recognised through the C3 rating by the Regulator of Social Housing and the move to carrying out a 100% stock condition survey to verify the current condition of the existing stock.

findings.paper_title: Housing Revenue Account Budget (including Rents & Other Charges for Council Dwellings) (Paper No. 26-7)
findings.headline: Repairs overspend of £9m in the current year, with no business plan assumption the elevated level will continue.
findings.detail: The council is forecasting a significant overspend predominantly in void repairs and fire/building safety remedial works. The business plan makes no allowance for these costs to continue at current elevated levels, which would require reprioritisation of existing commitments if they do.
findings.matters: Structural cost escalation in repairs is a leading indicator of whether the HRA business plan assumptions hold. Unplanned overspends at this scale must be funded from reserves or defer other planned investment.
findings.figures: £9m overspend forecast for the year; £9.6m in repairs and maintenance budget pressures above 'business as usual' baseline
findings.quote: Repairs budgets in the HRA have again been put under increasing pressure during this financial year and a significant overspend is again being forecast predominantly in relation to repairing and refurbishing vacant properties (voids) before they are re-let but also across general repairs, notably within building and fire safety as a consequence of remedial works identified as part of the stock condition survey acceleration.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Investments and Borrowing (Paper No. 25-423)
findings.headline: £670m housing regeneration borrowing depends on rental income and lettings policy assumptions
findings.detail: Wandsworth plans £670m of new borrowing over 10 years for estate regeneration and new housing. Affordability depends on 1,000 new homes generating projected rent and service charge income of £8.8m annually, combined with a policy of directing 45% of lettings to homeless queues (generating an estimated £9m annual saving in temporary accommodation costs). These are policy and market assumptions that could change.
findings.matters: Borrowing affordability is contingent on specific policy and market assumptions. If lettings to homeless populations fall below 45% or rents don't reach projected levels, revenue streams supporting £670m of debt could be materially impaired.
findings.figures: £670m new borrowing over 10 years; £8.8m annual rent/service charge income from 1,000 new homes; £9m annual temporary accommodation savings from 45% homeless lettings
findings.quote: For instance, the 1,000 homes being built will generate rent and service charge income of £8.8m per annum based on current average rents and service charges.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Investments and Borrowing (Paper No. 25-423)
findings.headline: Inflation and fire safety regulations force shift to borrowing for housing stock maintenance
findings.detail: Wandsworth's 33,000-home housing stock can no longer be maintained from routine capital financing resources. Inflation and fire/building safety regulatory requirements have increased maintenance costs beyond available funding. The council assumes £200m borrowing will be needed for capital repairs and improvements, averaging £61m annual spending over the next decade.
findings.matters: This represents a structural change in the council's financial position, moving from self-funded maintenance to debt-funded maintenance. Regulatory compliance costs are non-negotiable, and if inflation persists, borrowing requirements could grow further.
findings.figures: £200m borrowing assumed for existing stock maintenance; £61m average annual capital spend over next 10 years
findings.quote: Significant inflationary increases within the sector over the past few years plus increased regulatory requirements have meant the amounts being invested are now higher than the routine capital financing resources available to fund works to the existing stock, hence the current planned use of borrowing.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Mid Year Review 2025/26 (Paper No.25-419)
findings.paper_url: https://democracy.wandsworth.gov.uk/documents/s123803/25-419 Treasury Management Annual Report 2024-25 and Mid-year review 2025-26.pdf
findings.headline: Investment returns falling as Bank Rate declines, threatening council's financial cushion for demand-led service cost pressures
findings.detail: Weighted average return on investments has declined from 5.10% in 2024/25 to 4.48% as at 30 September 2025, and is expected to fall further to between 4.40% and 4.45% by year-end as the Bank Rate cuts flow through. The paper explicitly states that current treasury income is 'helping to offset cost pressures currently being experienced across the Council's demand led services'. As investment returns compress, the council's ability to absorb these pressures through treasury gains diminishes.
findings.matters: Lenders need to understand whether the council's financial position depends on sustained or declining income streams. Declining treasury returns reduce the council's financial flexibility at a time when it faces unexplained demand-led service cost pressures, potentially forcing spending cuts or borrowing.
findings.quote: The average return on investments was 5.10% in 2024/25 and so far in 2025/26 it is 4.48%.

findings.paper_title: Write off of Irrecoverable Debts over £25,000 (Paper No.25-422)
findings.headline: Two developers entered administration owing £1.3m in unpaid CIL, with recovery uncertain
findings.detail: Two developers entered administration leaving £1.3m in unpaid Borough Community Infrastructure Levy. The council states legal advisors have been engaged to 'protect and maximise the Council's position,' language that suggests recovery is not assured and may be partial.
findings.matters: Material CIL debt linked to developer insolvency signals stress in the development pipeline and creates uncertainty about ringfenced infrastructure funding
findings.figures: £1.3m in unpaid Borough CIL from two developers in administration
findings.quote: Two developers entered administration, leaving £1.3 million in unpaid Borough CIL. Legal advisors have been engaged to protect and maximise the Council's position.

findings.paper_title: Write off of Irrecoverable Debts over £25,000 (Paper No.25-422)
findings.headline: Housing Benefit Overpayment write-offs more than doubled to £1.5m in 2024/25
findings.detail: Write-offs surged from £619k in 2023/24 to £1.547m in 2024/25, a 150% increase. As a percentage of benefit payments made, write-offs rose from 0.45% to 1.18%. Outstanding debt stands at £16.726m. The paper describes this increase as reflecting 'additional work undertaken by the team to review old year debts,' suggesting accumulated unresolved cases are now being written off.
findings.matters: The jump in write-offs suggests the council finally reviewed legacy overpayments and found them unrecoverable, indicating past collection efforts were ineffective or the debtors' circumstances have deteriorated
findings.figures: £619k (2023/24) to £1.547m (2024/25); 1.18% of benefit payments; £16.726m outstanding
findings.quote: The number and value of debt write offs in 2024/25 is higher than in previous years but remains low comparative to the total value of HB payments made. This increase reflects the additional work undertaken by the team to review old year debts.

findings.paper_title: Write off of Irrecoverable Debts over £25,000 (Paper No.25-422)
findings.headline: Business Rates collection rate slipped to 97.5% with £5.3m aged debt over 6 years old
findings.detail: Business Rates in-year collection rate fell from a 98.56% target to 97.5% outturn in 2024/25. Of the £22.9m total outstanding business rates debt at end of March 2025, £5.3m (23% of total) is over six years old. The council notes a re-structure and extra resources are planned for 2026 to work older debts, suggesting backlog and staffing constraints.
findings.matters: Aged business rates arrears accumulating despite collection efforts indicates either business insolvency or the council's limited capacity to pursue older debts; either signals collection risk
findings.figures: £5.3m over 6 years old out of £22.9m total; collection rate 97.5% (target was 98.56%)
findings.quote: Of the £22.9m total debt at the end of March 2025, £6.4m (27%) of debt was under one year old and £9.8m (41%) under two years. Although aged debt is decreasing annually, £5.3m remains over six years old, with a lower likelihood of collection.

findings.paper_title: Write off of Irrecoverable Debts over £25,000 (Paper No.25-422)
findings.headline: Universal Credit deduction rules changing from April 2025 will reduce debt recovery from benefits
findings.detail: The Government's Fair Payment Rate reduces Universal Credit deductions for debt repayments from 25% to 15% from April 2025, allowing claimants to retain an average of £420 more annually. The council flags it will need to monitor the full impact on collection rates and arrears later in the year, implying it expects material deterioration.
findings.matters: This is a structural reduction in the council's ability to recover debts from the poorest residents, will increase arrears, and removes a collection lever the council has relied on
findings.figures: Universal Credit deductions reducing from 25% to 15%; claimants retaining an average of £420 more annually
findings.quote: From April 2025, the Government's Fair Payment Rate will reduce Universal Credit deductions for debt repayments from 25% to 15%, applying to debts owed to central and local government and utilities, with local authorities limited to rent, council tax arrears, and benefit overpayments. This allows claimants to repay over a longer period and retain an average of £420 more annually, with the full impact on collection rates and arrears to be seen later in the year.

findings.paper_title: Write off of Irrecoverable Debts over £25,000 (Paper No.25-422)
findings.headline: Council Tax outstanding debt rose 12.6% to £20.9m despite collection efforts
findings.detail: Council Tax debt outstanding increased from £18.526m in 2023/24 to £20.862m in 2024/25. In-year collection rate fell to 97.8%, below the 98.0% target. The paper cites the cost-of-living crisis as a factor, and notes the council has held back some write-offs pending access to HMRC data. The council is struggling to collect from financially stressed residents.
findings.matters: Deteriorating collection on the council's largest single tax base, combined with deliberate write-off deferral, signals both increased household hardship and the council's caution about which debts are recoverable
findings.figures: £20.862m outstanding (2024/25) vs £18.526m (2023/24); collection rate 97.8%
findings.quote: The cost-of-living crisis has also had an impact as more households are struggling to pay their bills. The Council monitors arrears carefully to decide upon the appropriate recovery options.

findings.paper_title: Write off of Irrecoverable Debts over £25,000 (Paper No.25-422)
findings.headline: Adult Social Care debt surged 69.8% to £30.4m in a single year
findings.detail: Outstanding Adult Social Care debt jumped from £17.856m at end of 2023/24 to £30.358m at end of 2024/25. As of July 2025, £19.2m remained outstanding, with £15.5m overdue beyond 30 days. The debt includes £6m in outstanding NHS invoices. The team wrote off only £346k despite the scale of arrears, suggesting collection difficulty rather than successful recovery.
findings.matters: A 70% surge in one year for a vulnerable population debt suggests the council's adult social care cost pressures or payment collection is deteriorating sharply, a potential leading indicator of budget stress
findings.figures: £17.856m (2023/24) to £30.358m (2024/25); £19.2m outstanding as of July 2025 with £15.5m overdue
findings.quote: At the end of July 2025, the level of outstanding Adult Social Care debt was £19.2m with the level of overdue debt that is over 30 days and not secured, at £15.5m. There remains outstanding NHS invoices to the value of £6m within that sum.

news_drafts.headline: Audit scale fees have increased 320% since 2021/22 and additional charges are expected
news_drafts.lead: Rising audit costs represent a material ongoing claim on the council's finances that lenders need to understand when assessing the council's cash position.
news_drafts.paper_title: 26-178 Update on Accounts and External Audit 2025-26

news_drafts.headline: Demand growth in social care, SEND and housing must be actively managed before planned MTFS savings can be realised
news_drafts.lead: Signals that MTFS savings targets may not be deliverable without proactive demand management action, raising execution risk around council's financial sustainability plans.
news_drafts.paper_title: Appendix B - Draft Annual Governance Statement 2025-26

news_drafts.headline: Fair Funding Review will reduce available funding with full impact phased from 2026/27 to 2028/29
news_drafts.lead: Specific, material reduction in government funding over defined period creates structural pressure on financial sustainability and will require service efficiencies or reductions to maintain current spending.
news_drafts.paper_title: Appendix B - Draft Annual Governance Statement 2025-26
